---
title: "Normalizing Flows"
---



[RBIG](02-rbig.qmd) builds the map $T$ from a *fixed* recipe — rank-Gaussianize,
then rotate.  A **normalizing flow** instead *learns* $T$: it composes many simple
invertible layers whose parameters are trained by maximum likelihood, so the map
can bend to dependence too rich for RBIG's fixed rotations.

## Same Spine, Learned Map

A flow is a chain of invertible transforms $T = T_K \circ \cdots \circ T_1$, each
with an easy Jacobian, trained so that $z = T(x)$ is standard Gaussian.  The
[change-of-variables](01-change-of-variables.qmd) formula gives the exact training
loss (the log-likelihood), and the *same* chain run backward, $x = T^{-1}(z)$,
generates samples — exactly the forward/backward spine, now with a flexible $T$.

| | RBIG | Normalizing flow |
|---|---|---|
| Map $T$ | fixed: rank-Gaussianize + rotate | learned invertible layers |
| Training | none (closed-form per layer) | maximum likelihood (gradient descent) |
| Capacity | limited by rotations | high; bends to rich dependence |
| Cost | cheap | training-heavy (GPU/JAX) |

## Fixed Recipe vs Learned Map

RBIG's map is a *fixed recipe*: rank-Gaussianize every marginal, then apply a
rotation, and loop.  Rotations are powerful but rigid — they can only *spin* the
cloud, never *bend* it.  When dependence is sharply curved, a rotation untangles
nothing: it just hands the next layer back a differently-oriented crescent.

A flow instead **learns** the invertible map $T_\theta$ by maximum likelihood, so
it can fold and stretch space until even a curved shape lands on a clean
$\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ ball.  The figure below is *illustrative* — two interlocking
moons are exactly the kind of shape no rotation can disentangle, and the learned
flow $T_\theta$ is the map that carries them, both ways, to and from the Gaussian
latent.

::: {#cell-fig-flow-moons .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)


def _moons(n):
    th = rng.uniform(0, np.pi, n)
    s = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
    mx = np.where(s == 0, np.cos(th), 1 - np.cos(th))
    my = np.where(s == 0, np.sin(th) - 0.25, 0.25 - np.sin(th))
    return np.column_stack([mx, my]) + rng.normal(0, 0.06, (n, 2))


fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
axL.scatter(*_moons(2500).T, s=7, c=WARM, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title(r"data  ·  too curved for rotations", fontsize=12)
axR.scatter(*rng.normal(size=(2500, 2)).T, s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title(r"latent  $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$", fontsize=12)
for a in (axL, axR):
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); despine(a)
fig.suptitle(r"learned flow  $T_\theta$:   data  $\rightleftarrows$  Gaussian", fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Illustrative. Data too curved for any rotation (left) and the Gaussian latent it is mapped to (right). The learned flow $T_\theta$ is the invertible map running data ⇌ Gaussian; a fixed rank-Gaussianize-and-rotate recipe cannot untangle this shape.](04-flows_files/figure-html/fig-flow-moons-output-1.png){#fig-flow-moons width=987 height=404}
:::
:::


A fixed rotation could never carry the moons onto that ball; a learned map can.
That extra capacity is the whole reason to reach for a flow — and it comes from
stacking one simple, invertible building block.

## The Building Block — The Coupling Layer

Each layer of a flow has to be *invertible* with a *cheap* Jacobian determinant,
because the [change-of-variables](01-change-of-variables.qmd) loss needs both.  The
**coupling layer** ([RealNVP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08803)) is the canonical
trick that gets both for free: split the coordinates into two halves $x_a, x_b$,
leave the first half untouched, and scale-and-shift the second half using small
networks $s(\cdot), t(\cdot)$ that see *only* the first half.

$$
\underbrace{\begin{aligned}
z_a &= x_a \\
z_b &= x_b \odot e^{s(x_a)} + t(x_a)
\end{aligned}}_{\text{forward}}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\underbrace{\begin{aligned}
x_a &= z_a \\
x_b &= \big(z_b - t(z_a)\big) \odot e^{-s(z_a)}
\end{aligned}}_{\text{inverse}}
$$

Inversion needs no network inverse — $s$ and $t$ are re-evaluated on the
*unchanged* half $z_a = x_a$, then we undo the affine step.  The Jacobian is
**triangular** (changing $x_a$ moves both outputs, but $x_b$ moves only $z_b$), so
its log-determinant is just the sum of the scale terms:

$$
\log\Big|\det \tfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\Big| = \sum_i s_i(x_a)\,.
$$

::: {#cell-fig-coupling .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 3.0))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 4); ax.axis("off")

box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", lw=1.6)
ax.text(0.9, 3.0, r"$x_a$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
        bbox={**box, "ec": COOL, "fc": "white"})
ax.text(0.9, 1.0, r"$x_b$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
        bbox={**box, "ec": WARM, "fc": "white"})
ax.text(4.8, 1.9, r"$s(x_a),\ t(x_a)$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12,
        bbox={**box, "ec": INK, "fc": plotting.PANEL})
ax.text(7.6, 1.0, r"$\odot\,e^{s}+t$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12,
        bbox={**box, "ec": INK, "fc": "white"})
ax.text(9.3, 3.0, r"$z_a = x_a$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
        bbox={**box, "ec": COOL, "fc": "white"})
ax.text(9.3, 1.0, r"$z_b$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
        bbox={**box, "ec": WARM, "fc": "white"})

arrow = dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.5)
ax.annotate("", xy=(8.4, 3.0), xytext=(1.9, 3.0), arrowprops=arrow)   # x_a → z_a (pass-through)
ax.annotate("", xy=(3.4, 1.9), xytext=(1.6, 2.7), arrowprops=arrow)   # x_a → net
ax.annotate("", xy=(7.0, 1.4), xytext=(6.2, 1.9), arrowprops=arrow)   # net → warp
ax.annotate("", xy=(6.9, 1.0), xytext=(1.9, 1.0), arrowprops=arrow)   # x_b → warp
ax.annotate("", xy=(8.4, 1.0), xytext=(8.5, 1.0), arrowprops=arrow)   # warp → z_b
ax.text(5.2, 3.25, "untouched half conditions the warp", ha="center",
        fontsize=10, color=INK, style="italic")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![One coupling layer. The first half passes through unchanged and conditions a small net $s, t$ that affinely warps the second half — invertible by construction, with a cheap triangular log-det.](04-flows_files/figure-html/fig-coupling-output-1.png){#fig-coupling width=968 height=344}
:::
:::


Stack many such layers — permuting which half is held fixed between them so every
coordinate eventually gets warped — and the chain becomes a flexible, fully
invertible $T_\theta$, trained end-to-end by maximum likelihood.  That is the
machinery [gauss_flows](https://github.com/jejjohnson/gauss_flows) (JAX/FlowJax)
provides.

## The Generative Direction, Illustrated

The render below uses `rbig`'s `AnnealedRBIG` as the stand-in generator — the
*behaviour* is what matters: draw a simple Gaussian sample, push it through the
learned inverse, and recover the data's joint tail.  A production flow
([gauss_flows](https://github.com/jejjohnson/gauss_flows), JAX/FlowJax) replaces
the stand-in but tells the same story.

::: {#cell-fig-flow-samples .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=1500, seed=2)
X = np.column_stack([a, b])
gen = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=1).fit(X).sample(len(X))

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4))
for ax, data, col, title in [
    (axL, X, COOL, f"real data · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(X[:,0], X[:,1]):.0%}"),
    (axR, gen, plotting.PALETTE["purple"],
     f"learned generator · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(gen[:,0], gen[:,1]):.0%}"),
]:
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=8, c=col, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
    ax.axvspan(-6, np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.1), color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.axhspan(-6, np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.1), color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlim(-5, 5); ax.set_ylim(-5, 5)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A learned generator: real data (left) and samples drawn backward through the map (right) share the joint tail dependence.](04-flows_files/figure-html/fig-flow-samples-output-1.png){#fig-flow-samples width=1304 height=512}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## When to Reach for a Flow
Use RBIG when its rotation-and-marginal structure already captures the
dependence — it is cheap and needs no training.  Reach for a flow when the
dependence is too intricate (sharp, multimodal, high-curvature) for fixed
rotations to disentangle, and you can afford to train.  Both are the same
invertible-map idea; the flow just buys capacity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Demo Hook
The course demo trains a real flow with `gauss_flows` (JAX) and compares its
samples and log-likelihoods to RBIG's — run it in the opt-in `demos` environment,
where the heavy libraries live.
:::

This closes the forward direction.  The same map, run **backward** as a risk
engine, is the subject of [Uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd).
